Huynh T.lab_name: Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine, and Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute, Texas Children's Hospital (Houston, Texas, USA)
Huynh T.role: Houston-based co-author on a long run of papers from Andrea Ballabio's group on TFEB, the master switch for lysosome and autophagy genes, including the work that tied TFEB to mTOR, starvation and fat metabolism
Huynh T.sub: Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine · Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute, Texas Children's Hospital (latest PubMed affiliation, 2026) · co-author with the Ballabio, Settembre and Sardiello groups (2011–2026)
story: Cells keep themselves clean with lysosomes, small acid-filled bags that break down worn-out parts, and with autophagy, the process that delivers those parts to the lysosome. In 2011 Carmine Settembre, Andrea Ballabio and colleagues, with Tuong Huynh among the co-authors, showed that one transcription factor, TFEB, switches on a whole programme of autophagy and lysosome genes when cells are starved (SET2011). In that first paper TFEB was controlled by the kinase ERK2. The 2012 follow-up (SET2012) found the link to mTORC1, the growth-control complex that sits on the lysosome surface: when nutrients are plentiful, mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB and keeps it out of the nucleus, so the lysosome itself reports its state to the genes that build it.

The 2013 paper (SET2013) moved into living mice. Fasting switched on the TFEB gene in liver, muscle and kidney, and TFEB then boosted its own production in a feed-forward loop. In the liver it drove fat breakdown largely through PGC-1alpha and PPARalpha, and extra liver TFEB protected mice from diet-induced obesity. The most recent paper (FER2026) used kidney-specific mouse models to separate mTORC1 activity from TFEB/TFE3 activity and found that overactive mTORC1, not TFEB/TFE3 alone, is the main driver of kidney cysts and tumours in models of Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome and tuberous sclerosis complex.

PubMed lists Tuong Huynh on about a dozen TFEB, lysosome and autophagy papers with the Ballabio, Settembre or Sardiello groups between 2011 and 2026. The early papers give no affiliation for this author; a 2020 paper and the 2026 kidney paper place Huynh at the Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine, and the Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute of Texas Children's Hospital in Houston, where Ballabio's US laboratory is based. The exact job title could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.SET2011: Co-author on the discovery that TFEB coordinates autophagy and lysosome genes during starvation.
highlights.SET2012: Co-author on the paper showing that mTOR-dependent phosphorylation of TFEB lets the lysosome signal its own state to the nucleus.
highlights.SET2013: Co-author on the mouse study showing that fasting turns on TFEB, which then drives its own gene and liver fat breakdown.
highlights.FER2026: Co-author on the kidney mouse models that identified mTORC1 overactivity as the main driver of cysts and tumours, with TFEB/TFE3 adding to it.

Lv S.lab_name: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
Lv S.role: Kidney researcher at Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, and first author of a 2026 study tracing a chain of enzymes that switches on mTOR and drives scarring in damaged kidneys
Lv S.sub: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Chronic kidney disease often ends in fibrosis, a slow scarring in which working kidney tissue is replaced by stiff connective tissue. In the 2026 study led by Shiqi Lv, with Xiaoyan Zhang as senior author, the team followed a chain of four molecules. USP7 is a deubiquitinase, an enzyme that removes ubiquitin tags, the labels that send proteins to be destroyed. By removing them from KDM5B, USP7 keeps KDM5B stable. KDM5B is a histone demethylase, an enzyme that strips activating marks from the proteins that package DNA, and here it silences the gene for TSC1. TSC1 is part of the brake on mTOR, so less TSC1 means more mTOR activity and more scarring.

The evidence comes from two mouse models of kidney injury, where blocking USP7 genetically or with a drug restored TSC1, damped mTOR and reduced fibrosis, and from human kidney samples, where USP7 levels were higher in chronic kidney disease and tracked with how much scarring was present. The human part is a correlation; the cause-and-effect steps were shown in mice and cells.

PubMed lists Shiqi Lv at the Department of Nephrology of Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, in Shanghai. No official profile page could be checked, so the current position is given as at the time of the study.

highlights.LV2026S: First author: showed that USP7 stabilizes KDM5B, which silences TSC1 and activates mTOR, driving kidney fibrosis in mice; USP7 was raised in human CKD kidneys.

Zhang Xiaoyan.lab_name: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (Shanghai, China)
Zhang Xiaoyan.role: Nephrologist at Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, and senior author of a 2026 study linking the enzyme USP7 to mTOR activation and kidney scarring
Zhang Xiaoyan.sub: Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Xiaoyan Zhang is the senior author of a 2026 study on kidney fibrosis, the scarring that slowly destroys function in chronic kidney disease. The team, with Shiqi Lv as first author, described a chain of control. The enzyme USP7 removes destruction tags from KDM5B, an enzyme that edits the chemical marks on DNA packaging proteins. Stable KDM5B shuts down the gene for TSC1, one half of the main brake on mTOR, and mTOR activity then rises and promotes scarring.

Blocking USP7, by deleting it or with a drug, brought TSC1 back, lowered mTOR activity and reduced fibrosis in two mouse models of kidney injury. In human kidney biopsies USP7 was higher in chronic kidney disease and rose with the amount of scarring, which is an association rather than proof of cause. The authors propose the USP7-KDM5B-TSC1-mTOR axis as a possible drug target.

PubMed gives the Department of Nephrology, Zhongshan Hospital, Fudan University, Shanghai, as the affiliation. Because Xiaoyan Zhang is a very common name, no wider publication record or career details are given here without a second independent link.

highlights.LV2026S: Senior author: led the study showing that the USP7-KDM5B axis silences TSC1, activates mTOR and promotes kidney fibrosis in mice, with supporting correlations in human CKD tissue.

Zhang Xiaoyan.note: Very common name; no career details added beyond the Atlas paper's affiliation.

Feng H.lab_name: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou, Jiangsu, China)
Feng H.role: Neurologist at Suzhou Municipal Hospital and senior author of a 2026 stroke study proposing PIP4K2A as a protector of brain tissue through AKT/mTOR signalling and autophagy
Feng H.sub: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou Municipal Hospital), Gusu School, Nanjing Medical University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: When a stroke blocks a brain artery, doctors try to restore blood flow as quickly as possible. The returning blood, however, causes a second wave of damage called ischemia/reperfusion injury. The 2026 study led by Bodun Ma, with Hongxuan Feng as senior author, looked at PIP4K2A, a lipid kinase, in laboratory models of this injury.

Raising PIP4K2A levels reduced the injury. The team linked the effect to two things: less of a TRIB3-p62 protein complex, which can clog autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and changed AKT/mTOR signalling, so that autophagy could run properly again. The study proposes PIP4K2A-AKT/mTOR as a protective axis, a result from experimental models that has not been tested in patients.

PubMed lists Hongxuan Feng at the Department of Neurology of the Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University. No official profile could be checked, so the position is given as at the time of the study.

highlights.MA2026: Senior author: led the study showing that PIP4K2A lessens ischemia/reperfusion brain injury by reducing the TRIB3-p62 complex and adjusting AKT/mTOR signalling to restore autophagy.

Ma B.lab_name: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou, Jiangsu, China)
Ma B.role: Neurology researcher in Suzhou and first author of a 2026 study on how the enzyme PIP4K2A protects the brain after stroke by restoring autophagy through AKT/mTOR
Ma B.sub: Department of Neurology, The Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (Suzhou Municipal Hospital), Gusu School, Nanjing Medical University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Restoring blood flow after a stroke saves brain tissue, but the sudden return of oxygen also injures cells. Bodun Ma's 2026 study, with Hongxuan Feng as senior author, asked whether the lipid kinase PIP4K2A could limit this reperfusion damage.

In the team's experimental models, more PIP4K2A meant less injury. Two changes went with it: less of a TRIB3-p62 complex that can jam autophagy, the cell's recycling pathway, and altered AKT/mTOR signalling, which let autophagy flow again. mTOR normally holds autophagy back when growth signals are high, so tuning this pathway changes how well damaged neurons clear debris. These are laboratory findings, not results in stroke patients.
PubMed gives the Department of Neurology at the Affiliated Suzhou Hospital of Nanjing Medical University as Bodun Ma's affiliation. A current position could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.MA2026: First author: showed that PIP4K2A overexpression reduces ischemia/reperfusion brain injury by lowering the TRIB3-p62 burden and modulating AKT/mTOR to restore autophagic flux.

Granholm AC.lab_name: Department of Neurosurgery, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (Aurora, Colorado, USA)
Granholm AC.role: Neuroscientist of aging who has studied Down syndrome and the Alzheimer's disease that often comes with it since the 1990s, now a professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus
Granholm AC.sub: Professor, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus · founding Executive Director, Knoebel Institute for Healthy Aging, University of Denver (from 2015) · Director, Center on Aging, Medical University of South Carolina (14 years) · guest professor in neurosciences, Karolinska Institutet
story: People with Down syndrome carry three copies of chromosome 21, which includes the gene for amyloid precursor protein, and Alzheimer's disease brain changes are common as they age. The 2026 study led by Abigail Nordbeck, with Ann-Charlotte Granholm as senior author, looked at post-mortem hippocampus, the brain's memory hub, from people with Down syndrome and Alzheimer's neuropathology. Using spatial transcriptomics, which reads gene activity while keeping track of where in the tissue it happens, and localized proteomics, the team found that mTOR pathway signalling was altered in particular hippocampal subfields, while insulin signalling was altered mainly in the dentate granule neurons.

The point is that the changes were not uniform across the tissue. Different cell layers showed different disturbances in the two growth and nutrient pathways. The authors call these preliminary observations from a small set of human brains; they describe associations, not causes.

Granholm holds both a dental degree (DDS) and a PhD and has held NIH R01 funding for Down syndrome research since 1994. At the Medical University of South Carolina she directed the Center on Aging for 14 years and the brain bank. In 2015 she moved to the University of Denver as founding executive director of the Knoebel Institute for Healthy Aging, and she holds a guest professorship in neurosciences at the Karolinska Institutet. The group studies healthy aging and age-related neurodegeneration, especially Down syndrome-related Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, using biomarkers, neuropathology and animal models. Granholm is now a professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and part of the Down Syndrome Biobank Consortium run from its Department of Neurosurgery; publications also appear under the names Ann-Charlotte Granholm-Bentley and Lotta Granholm.

highlights.NOR2026: Senior author: led the spatial study of human post-mortem hippocampus showing subfield-specific mTOR and cell-type-specific insulin pathway changes in Down syndrome with Alzheimer's neuropathology.

Granholm AC.note: Department: PubMed (2026) says Neurology, CU Medicine provider page lists her as Professor of Neurology under the neurosurgery section, and the biobank page sits under Neurosurgery; lab_name uses Neurosurgery, curator may prefer Neurology. Source pages use 'she/her'; story uses it once. Degree institutions not found.

Pirscoveanu DF.lab_name: Department of Neurology, University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova (Craiova, Romania)
Pirscoveanu DF.role: Neurology researcher in Craiova who works with Aurel Popa-Wagner on aging and stroke, and first author of a 2026 review on why mTOR-type lifespan gains shrink from worms to mammals
Pirscoveanu DF.sub: Department of Neurology, University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova (2026) · Chair of Vascular Neurology, Dementia and Ageing, University Hospital Essen (2025 affiliation)
story: Blocking TOR, the yeast and worm version of mTOR, can lengthen the life of a roundworm several-fold, yet rapamycin extends mouse lifespan by a much smaller fraction. The 2026 review led by Denisa Pirscoveanu, with Aurel Popa-Wagner as senior author, asks why. It compares data from the worm C. elegans, the fruit fly and rodents and argues that in simple animals aging is steered by a few high-leverage pathways, while in mammals it is spread across many tissues with backup systems, feedback, hormones, gut microbes and the complications of getting a drug to the right place in the body.

The authors call this a shift from pathway leverage to system-level buffering. It is a synthesis of earlier results, not a new experiment, and it gives a framework for why a pathway like mTOR can matter a great deal in mammals while any single drug still has a limited effect on lifespan.

PubMed places Pirscoveanu in the Department of Neurology at the University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova in 2026 and, in 2025, at the Chair of Vascular Neurology, Dementia and Ageing of University Hospital Essen, University of Duisburg-Essen, where Popa-Wagner also works. Their joint papers since 2025 include work on immune genes and post-stroke damage in the aging rat brain.

highlights.PIR2026: First author: wrote the cross-species review arguing that TOR-pathway lifespan gains fall in mammals because aging there is buffered across many tissues and systems.

Popa-Wagner A.lab_name: Department of Neurology, University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova (Craiova, Romania)
Popa-Wagner A.role: Neuroscientist of brain aging and stroke recovery working between Craiova and Essen, senior author of a 2026 review on the limits of extending lifespan through the mTOR pathway
Popa-Wagner A.sub: Department of Neurology, University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova · Chair of Vascular Neurology, Dementia and Ageing, University Hospital Essen, University of Duisburg-Essen
story: In worms and flies, turning down TOR signalling can stretch lifespan dramatically. In mice, rapamycin also works, but the gain is far smaller. The 2026 review led by Denisa Pirscoveanu, with Aurel Popa-Wagner as senior author, offers an explanation: in simple organisms aging runs through a few dominant pathways, whereas in mammals it emerges from many organs talking to each other, with redundant genes, hormonal feedback, gut microbes and drug-handling differences that soften the effect of any single intervention.

For readers of this Atlas the useful message is about expectations. mTOR remains a central aging pathway in mammals, but the review argues that its leverage is diluted by system-level buffering. The paper is a synthesis of published data across species, not a new experiment.

PubMed lists Popa-Wagner at both the Department of Neurology of the University of Medicine and Pharmacy of Craiova and the Chair of Vascular Neurology, Dementia and Ageing at University Hospital Essen. Recent papers with this group study stroke in the aging rat brain, for example how immune genes active during early brain development contribute to post-stroke damage in old male rats.

highlights.PIR2026: Senior author: led the cross-species review proposing that mTOR-pathway lifespan gains shrink in mammals because of multi-tissue buffering and redundancy.

Popa-Wagner A.note: Training and earlier career not researched (web search budget ran out); worth a later check of an official Craiova or Essen page.

Huang W.lab_name: Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
Huang W.role: Neuroscientist trained in Mauro Costa-Mattioli's memory lab at Baylor, first author of the study that showed mTORC2 is needed for long-term memory through control of the actin skeleton
Huang W.sub: Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (latest PubMed affiliation, 2017) · Department of Neuroscience and Memory and Brain Research Center, Baylor College of Medicine (Costa-Mattioli lab, 2011–2017)
story: Long-term memories need new proteins, and most memory work on mTOR had focused on mTORC1, the complex that drives protein synthesis. Wei Huang's 2013 Nature Neuroscience paper, with Mauro Costa-Mattioli as senior author, looked at the other complex, mTORC2. Deleting its essential partner Rictor in the mouse forebrain after birth lowered mTORC2 activity and selectively impaired long-term memory and the late, protein-dependent phase of long-term potentiation (LTP), the strengthening of synapses thought to store memories. Flies lacking TORC2 showed a similar long-term memory defect.

The team traced the problem to actin, the protein filaments that shape dendritic spines, the small knobs where synapses sit. Actin polymerisation was reduced in the mutant hippocampus, and restoring it rescued both late LTP and long-term memory. A compound that raised mTORC2 activity turned short-lasting LTP into the long-lasting form and improved memory in normal mice. The work showed that mTORC2, not only mTORC1, is needed to consolidate long-term memories.

Huang's PubMed record with Costa-Mattioli runs from 2011 to 2017 and includes a pharmacogenetic study showing mTORC1 is required for late LTP and memory storage (2011) and a 2016 eLife paper showing that translational control by eIF2alpha phosphorylation explains why adolescent mice are more sensitive to cocaine. A 2017 paper lists Huang at both Baylor and the Solomon H. Snyder Department of Neuroscience at Johns Hopkins. The current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.HUA2013: First author: showed that forebrain mTORC2 loss impairs long-term memory and late LTP through reduced actin polymerisation, and that boosting mTORC2 enhances memory.

Nordbeck AJ.lab_name: Department of Neurosurgery, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (Aurora, Colorado, USA)
Nordbeck AJ.role: Neuroscience researcher and first author of a 2026 spatial study of the human hippocampus in Down syndrome with Alzheimer's disease, which found mTOR and insulin signalling disturbed in specific cell layers
Nordbeck AJ.sub: Department of Neurosurgery, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Almost everyone with Down syndrome has an extra copy of the amyloid precursor protein gene on chromosome 21, and Alzheimer's disease changes in the brain are common as they age. Abigail Nordbeck's 2026 study, with Ann-Charlotte Granholm as senior author, examined post-mortem hippocampus, the brain region central to forming memories, from people with Down syndrome and Alzheimer's neuropathology.

The team combined spatial transcriptomics, which measures gene activity while keeping its location in the tissue, with localized proteomics, which measures proteins in small chosen regions. mTOR pathway signalling was significantly altered in particular hippocampal subfields, and insulin pathway signalling was altered mainly in dentate granule neurons. In other words, the disturbance is local and cell-type specific rather than spread evenly through the tissue. The authors present these as preliminary observations in human tissue; they show associations and cannot say whether the changes cause the disease or follow from it.
PubMed lists Nordbeck at the Department of Neurosurgery of the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus for this study. A current position could not be confirmed from an official page.

Shimada H.lab_name: Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (Aurora, Colorado, USA)
Shimada H.role: Obstetrician-scientist from Sapporo Medical University working in the Colorado placenta group of Thomas Jansson, Theresa Powell and Fredrick Rosario on how mTOR controls nutrient transport to the fetus
Shimada H.sub: Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus (2024–2026) · Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Sapporo Medical University
story: The placenta decides how much food reaches a growing baby, and mTORC1, the cell's nutrient and growth sensor, helps set how fast it pumps amino acids across. In the 2026 study led by Hiroshi Shimada, with Fredrick Rosario as senior author, the team compared 46 placentas from healthy term pregnancies. Placentas from boys showed stronger mTORC1 signalling, more System A amino acid transport and higher mitochondrial respiration than placentas from girls, and boys had a higher birth weight relative to placental weight.

This was a snapshot at one time point with no treatment, so it shows an association between fetal sex and placental function, not a cause. It does suggest that male and female pregnancies may need to be analysed separately in placental research.

Shimada is listed by PubMed with both the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and Sapporo Medical University in Japan. Earlier work in the Colorado group includes a 2024 review on how placental amino acid transporters are regulated, with mTOR as a key regulator, and a 2025 mouse study in which switching off mTOR only in placental trophoblast cells cut the transport of folate to the fetus and reduced fetal growth.

highlights.SHIMADA2026: First author: compared 46 term placentas and found higher mTORC1 signalling, amino acid transport and mitochondrial respiration in placentas from male pregnancies.

Zhu L.lab_name: Department of Occupational Health and Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Anhui Medical University (Hefei, China)
Zhu L.role: Environmental health researcher at Anhui Medical University and first author of a 2026 mouse study on how the solvent trichloroethylene damages the liver when the LKB1/AMPK energy sensor is missing
Zhu L.sub: Department of Occupational Health and Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Anhui Medical University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Trichloroethylene is an industrial solvent used to degrease metal, and workers exposed to it can develop liver injury. Lifu Zhu's 2026 study, with J. Zhang as senior author, asked why some livers are hit harder. The focus was LKB1 and AMPK, a pair of enzymes that sense low energy in the cell and normally hold mTOR in check.

In mice lacking LKB1/AMPK, trichloroethylene caused worse liver injury. mTOR-regulated mitophagy, the clean-up of damaged mitochondria, failed, and mitochondrial DNA leaked out of the mitochondria, where it can trigger inflammation. Rapamycin, which blocks mTOR, and drugs that activate AMPK protected the liver. The work is in mice only, with no human data, and suggests the LKB1/AMPK/mTOR axis as a possible target.

PubMed lists Lifu Zhu at the Department of Occupational Health and Environmental Health, School of Public Health, Anhui Medical University in Hefei. A current position could not be confirmed from an official page.

highlights.ZHU2026: First author: showed in mice that LKB1/AMPK loss worsens trichloroethylene liver injury by impairing mTOR-regulated mitophagy, and that rapamycin or AMPK activation protects.

Pollizzi KN.lab_name: Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Department of Oncology, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Baltimore, Maryland, USA)
Pollizzi KN.role: Immunologist trained in Jonathan Powell's lab at Johns Hopkins who used gene deletions in mice to show how the two mTOR complexes push killer T cells toward effector or memory fates
Pollizzi KN.sub: Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Powell lab, 2011–2016; latest PubMed affiliation)
story: CD8 T cells are the immune system's killer cells. After an infection, most become short-lived effectors that attack, and a few become long-lived memory cells that guard against the next infection. Kristen Pollizzi's 2015 study in the Journal of Clinical Investigation, with Jonathan Powell as senior author, used mice whose T cells lacked Tsc2, Rheb or Rictor to separate the roles of the two mTOR complexes. With Tsc2 gone, mTORC1 stayed switched on: the cells burned glucose hard, made more of the killing molecules IFN-gamma, TNF and granzyme B, and controlled tumours better, but they ended up terminally differentiated, fewer in number after a month, and formed no memory. With Rheb gone, mTORC1 was off while mTORC2 still worked: these cells failed as effectors and kept memory-like features, yet they did not respond when the mice met the same antigen again, which the authors traced to defects in their metabolism.

The message is that mTOR activity tunes the balance between attack and memory, and that a T cell needs the right amount of each complex at the right time. That matters for vaccine design and for cancer treatments that rely on T cells. Pollizzi was also a co-author on the 2011 Nature Immunology paper from the same lab showing that mTORC1 and mTORC2 steer helper (CD4) T cells into different lineages.

PubMed lists 11 papers for Pollizzi between 2011 and 2016, all with the Powell group at the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Johns Hopkins. They include a 2015 PLoS One study showing that cell size after activation can be used to track mTOR activity and predict whether a T cell becomes an effector or a long-lived cell, and reviews on mTOR and T cell metabolism in Nature Reviews Immunology (2014) and Trends in Immunology (2015). No later publications or current position could be found.

highlights.POL2015: First author: used Tsc2, Rheb and Rictor deletion in T cells to show that constant mTORC1 drives glycolytic, terminally differentiated effectors with no memory, while loss of mTORC1 gives memory-like cells that still fail on rechallenge.
highlights.DEL2011: Co-author on the study showing that mTORC1 and mTORC2 selectively program distinct CD4 helper T-cell lineages.

Pollizzi KN.note: No publications after 2016 and no current position found; earlier profile text used 'she' without a source, removed.

Waickman AT.lab_name: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, SUNY Upstate Medical University (Syracuse, New York, USA)
Waickman AT.role: Immunologist who trained in Jonathan Powell's mTOR and T cell lab at Johns Hopkins and now studies human immune responses to dengue virus at SUNY Upstate Medical University
Waickman AT.sub: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, SUNY Upstate Medical University (2026 PubMed affiliation) · Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine (Powell lab, around 2011–2016)
story: Adam Waickman appears in this Atlas on two papers from Jonathan Powell's laboratory at Johns Hopkins that split T cell decisions between the two mTOR complexes. The 2011 Nature Immunology paper showed that mTORC1 and mTORC2 steer helper (CD4) T cells into different lineages. The 2015 Journal of Clinical Investigation paper did the same for killer (CD8) T cells: constant mTORC1 activity, after deleting Tsc2, produced aggressive but short-lived effector cells with no memory, while removing mTORC1 activity by deleting Rheb gave memory-like cells that still responded poorly to a second encounter with the antigen.

In the same period Waickman co-authored a 2015 PLoS One study from the lab showing that, within one batch of freshly activated CD4 T cells, the larger cells with high mTOR activity become glycolytic effector cells, while the smaller cells with low mTOR activity tend to become long-lived cells and regulatory T cells, a pattern also seen in human T cells.

PubMed lists close to 70 papers under Waickman's name. The recent ones come from the Department of Microbiology and Immunology at SUNY Upstate Medical University in Syracuse and deal with human immunity to dengue virus, including a 2026 Lancet Microbe report on a first-in-human dengue serotype 4 challenge study run with the University of Maryland and the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research. The exact title and lab page could not be checked.

highlights.POL2015: Co-author on the study showing that mTORC1 activity drives effector CD8 T cells at the expense of memory.
highlights.DEL2011: Co-author on the study showing that mTORC1 and mTORC2 selectively program distinct CD4 helper T-cell lineages.

Zhou N.lab_name: Department of Oncology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University (Harbin, China)
Zhou N.role: Oncology researcher at the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University and first author of a 2026 study linking a DNA-demethylating enzyme to PI3K-AKT-mTOR activation in lung adenocarcinoma
Zhou N.sub: Department of Oncology, The First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Genes can be silenced by methyl groups attached to their DNA, and enzymes called TET remove those marks to turn genes back on. Nan Zhou's 2026 study, with Y. Wang as senior author, found that in lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, TET1 strips the methyl marks from the control region of the MRPS17 gene. MRPS17 normally helps build the protein-making machinery inside mitochondria, and its overproduction in tumour cells switched on PI3K-AKT-mTOR signalling, a growth pathway, and made the cells divide, move and invade more.

Reducing MRPS17 pushed cancer cells into apoptosis, programmed cell death, and slowed tumour growth in cell culture and in animal experiments. The study ties an epigenetic switch to the mTOR growth pathway in one cancer type; it has not been tested in patients.
PubMed lists Nan Zhou at the Department of Oncology of the First Affiliated Hospital of Harbin Medical University. Because the name is common, no wider publication record is attributed here.

highlights.ZHOU2026: First author: showed that TET1-driven demethylation raises MRPS17 in lung adenocarcinoma, activating PI3K-AKT-mTOR and promoting tumour growth.

Zhou N.note: Common name; no career details beyond the Atlas paper.

Xu J.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Xu J.role: Researcher in the orthopedics department of Tongji Hospital, Wuhan, and first author of a 2026 review on mTORC2 and its partner RICTOR in immune cells and inflammatory disease
Xu J.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: Most writing on mTOR is about mTORC1, the complex that drives growth. Jingting Xu's 2026 review in Inflammation Research, with Fengjing Guo as senior author, collects what is known about the second complex, mTORC2, and its defining partner RICTOR in the immune system. mTORC2 acts through the kinases AKT, SGK1 and PKC.

The review describes how mTORC2 shapes the choice between Th1 and Th2 helper T cells, keeps regulatory T cells stable, helps memory T cells form, and affects B-cell receptor signalling, plasma cell survival, and the behaviour of macrophages, dendritic cells and natural killer cells. In tissues its effect depends on context: it worsens inflammation in osteoarthritis and pancreatitis but restrains pro-inflammatory macrophages in colorectal cancer. Drugs that block both mTOR complexes, such as AZD2014, show early but complicated promise. The paper is a review of published work, not new data.

story: Fengjing Guo is the senior author of a 2026 review, led by Jingting Xu, on mTORC2, the less studied of the two mTOR complexes, and its essential partner RICTOR. mTORC2 passes its signals through the kinases AKT, SGK1 and PKC, and the review follows these signals through T cells, B cells, macrophages, dendritic cells and natural killer cells.

One theme of the review is relevant to an orthopedics department: mTORC2 signalling makes inflammation worse in osteoarthritis, the joint disease in which cartilage wears away, and in pancreatitis, yet it restrains pro-inflammatory macrophages in colorectal cancer. The authors conclude that dual mTORC1/2 inhibitors such as AZD2014 show early but complicated promise. The paper summarises published studies and adds no new experiments.

You H.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
You H.role: Orthopedic researcher at Tongji Hospital, Wuhan, and senior author of a 2026 mouse study showing that the plant compound corilagin slows osteoarthritis by restoring cartilage-cell autophagy
You H.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Tongji Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: In osteoarthritis the cartilage that cushions joints slowly breaks down. Chondrocytes, the cells that maintain cartilage, depend on autophagy, their internal recycling system, and autophagy falls when PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling is too high. The 2026 study led by Ruijia Zhou, with Hongbo You as senior author, tested corilagin, a polyphenol found in several medicinal plants.

Corilagin lowered PI3K/AKT/mTOR and NF-kappaB signalling, the second being a main switch for inflammation. Chondrocytes recovered their autophagic flux and made more extracellular matrix, the material that gives cartilage its strength. In mice with surgically induced osteoarthritis (the DMM model, in which a knee ligament is cut to destabilise the joint), corilagin reduced cartilage erosion and lowered OARSI damage scores. These are cell and mouse results; corilagin has not been tested in people with osteoarthritis.

PubMed lists Hongbo You at the Department of Orthopedics of Tongji Hospital in Wuhan, where You has co-authored papers with Fengjing Guo, senior author of the Atlas review on mTORC2 in inflammation. Career details could not be confirmed from an official page.

story: Ruijia Zhou's 2026 study, with Hongbo You as senior author, looked for a way to protect cartilage in osteoarthritis. Cartilage cells, called chondrocytes, need autophagy to clear damaged parts, and too much PI3K/AKT/mTOR signalling holds autophagy back. Inflammation driven by NF-kappaB adds to the damage.

Corilagin, a polyphenol from several medicinal plants, damped both PI3K/AKT/mTOR and NF-kappaB in chondrocytes. Autophagy recovered and the cells produced more extracellular matrix, the tough material of cartilage. In mice whose knee joints were destabilised surgically (the DMM model), corilagin reduced cartilage erosion and joint damage scores. The results come from cells and mice only.

Chen Xianglong.lab_name: Department of Orthopedics, Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (Wuhan, Hubei, China)
Chen Xianglong.role: Orthopedic researcher at Union Hospital, Wuhan, and first author of a 2026 study that found a new route by which failing autophagy switches on mTORC1 and drives spinal disc degeneration
Chen Xianglong.sub: Department of Orthopedics, Union Hospital, Tongji Medical College, Huazhong University of Science and Technology (at the time of the study, 2026)
story: The discs between the vertebrae act as shock absorbers, and their slow degeneration is a major cause of back pain. Xianglong Chen's 2026 study in Advanced Science, with Y. Zhang as senior author, focused on chaperone-mediated autophagy, a selective clean-up route in which single proteins are fed one by one into the lysosome through a receptor called LAMP2A.

In disc cells from patients and in rat models, this pathway was weakened. One of its usual cargoes, the protein midnolin, then built up. Midnolin bound TSC2, part of the main brake on mTORC1, and sent it to the proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, without the usual ubiquitin tag. With the brake gone, mTORC1 became overactive, and the disc cells became senescent, released inflammatory signals and lost their matrix. Reducing midnolin, adding back LAMP2A or giving rapamycin each blocked the damage in cells and rats. The study describes a new upstream route to mTORC1 overactivity; it has not been tested as a treatment in people.

Nath P.lab_name: Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, LSU Health Shreveport (Shreveport, Louisiana, USA)
Nath P.role: Cancer researcher in Cherie-Ann Nathan's head and neck cancer group at LSU Health Shreveport, first author of a 2026 study showing that the mTOR inhibitor everolimus can turn immune-cold tumours hot in mice
Nath P.sub: Department of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery, LSU Health Shreveport (2024–2026, Nathan lab)
story: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma with a mutated TP53 gene often resists immunotherapy because the tumours are immune-cold: few killer T cells get inside. Priyatosh Nath's 2026 study, with Cherie-Ann Nathan as senior author, tested whether blocking mTOR could change that. A preprint version appeared on bioRxiv in June 2026 and the paper was then published in Neoplasia.

In mouse tumours of this type, including lines resistant to anti-PD-1 therapy, everolimus, an approved mTOR inhibitor, slowed tumour growth and remodelled the tumour surroundings. More CD8 T cells and dendritic cells came in, regulatory T cells that dampen immunity went down, and the HIF-1alpha/VEGFA signal that recruits immune-suppressing myeloid cells and builds blood vessels was reduced. Everolimus also raised the chemokine signals TNF-alpha and CXCL10 and lowered PD-1 and PD-L1, which helped T cells kill again. These are mouse results; the authors propose testing everolimus with immunotherapy in patients likely to fail immunotherapy alone.

Zong Y.role: Pathologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who works on the diagnosis of kidney and genitourinary tumours, senior author of a 2026 study proposing GPR143 as a marker for kidney tumours driven by the FLCN/TSC/mTOR-TFE pathway
Zong Y.sub: Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, University of Wisconsin-Madison (by 2024 to present) · Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, University of California Los Angeles (earlier)
story: Some kidney tumours are driven by faults in one signalling chain: the genes FLCN, TSC1/TSC2 and MTOR, which control mTORC1, and the TFE family of transcription factors that sit downstream. These tumours can look like other kidney cancers under the microscope, and getting the diagnosis right matters for treatment and for spotting inherited syndromes such as Birt-Hogg-Dube and tuberous sclerosis complex. The 2026 study in Virchows Archiv, led by Q. Li with Yang Zong as senior author, tested GPR143, a protein that can be stained in tissue sections.

GPR143 staining was both sensitive and specific for renal tumours with FLCN/TSC/MTOR-TFE alterations, which makes it a practical addition to the tests pathologists already use. The study is based on human tumour samples and is a diagnostic tool, not a treatment.

Zong was at the Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine of the University of California Los Angeles, where a 2024 Modern Pathology paper as first author described the genetic diversity of embryonic-type neuroectodermal tumours arising from testicular germ cell tumours; that paper notes the move to the University of Wisconsin-Madison. In Madison Zong also co-authored a 2026 study on the CXCL13-CXCR5 signal that draws CD8 T cells into clear cell renal cell carcinoma. A lab or profile page could not be checked.

highlights.LI2026: Senior author: led the study showing that GPR143 immunostaining is a sensitive and specific marker for renal tumours with FLCN/TSC/MTOR-TFE pathway alterations.

Dorrello NV.lab_name: Division of Pediatric Critical Care Medicine and Hospital Medicine, Department of Pediatrics, Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons (New York, New York, USA)
Dorrello NV.role: Pediatric critical care physician-scientist at Columbia University whose training in Michele Pagano's lab at NYU showed how S6K1 removes the translation brake PDCD4, and who now works on repairing injured children's lungs
Dorrello NV.sub: Division of Pediatric Critical Care Medicine and Hospital Medicine, Department of Pediatrics, Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons · Department of Pathology, NYU Cancer Institute, New York University School of Medicine (Pagano lab, 2003–2008)
story: To grow, a cell must make proteins, and to make proteins it must unwind the folded start of each messenger RNA. The helicase eIF4A does this, and the tumour suppressor PDCD4 holds eIF4A back. In 2006, in a Science paper with Michele Pagano as senior author, N. Valerio Dorrello showed how growth signals lift this brake. S6K1, a kinase switched on by mTORC1, phosphorylates PDCD4, which marks it for the ubiquitin ligase betaTRCP; PDCD4 is then destroyed, eIF4A is freed and translation and cell growth go up.

The paper added a new branch to the map of what mTORC1 does: besides acting on ribosomal protein S6 and on 4E-BP1, the pathway also removes an inhibitor of the translation machinery. Because PDCD4 is a tumour suppressor, its loss through this route also links mTOR signalling to cancer growth.

Dorrello's PubMed record has papers with the Pagano group at NYU from 2003 to 2008, then a later line of work at Columbia University. The later papers come from the Department of Pediatrics and its Division of Pediatric Critical Care Medicine, often with bioengineers, for example a 2017 study with Gordana Vunjak-Novakovic on delivering and imaging stem cells in the lung. As senior author of a 2026 npj Regenerative Medicine paper, Dorrello showed that healthy alveolar type II cells, the cells that make surfactant, can be engrafted into mice lacking surfactant protein C and reduce lung injury, a step toward cell therapy for childhood interstitial lung disease.

highlights.DOR2006: First author: showed that S6K1 triggers betaTRCP-mediated degradation of PDCD4, releasing the translation helicase eIF4A and promoting protein synthesis and cell growth.

Johnson SC.lab_name: School of Geography and Natural Sciences, Northumbria University (Newcastle upon Tyne, England, United Kingdom)
Johnson SC.role: Biologist of aging and mitochondrial disease, first author with Peter Rabinovitch and Matt Kaeberlein of the 2013 Nature review that made the case for mTOR as a central controller of aging, now a professor at Northumbria University
Johnson SC.sub: Professor, School of Geography and Natural Sciences, Northumbria University · Assistant Professor of Neurology, University of Washington, and Principal Investigator, Center for Integrative Brain Research, Seattle Children's Research Institute (earlier) · postdoc in Genetics, Albert Einstein College of Medicine · PhD in Molecular Basis of Disease, University of Washington (2013)
story: In 2013, while a PhD student in the Department of Pathology at the University of Washington, Simon Johnson was first author of the Nature review "mTOR is a key modulator of ageing and age-related disease", with Matt Kaeberlein as senior author. The review gathered the evidence that turning down mTOR signalling, genetically or with rapamycin, extends lifespan in model organisms from yeast to mice, and that it protects against a growing list of age-related diseases in animal models. It was also frank about the problem: side effects of the existing drugs stood in the way of giving them to healthy people. The paper became a standard starting map for the field.

Johnson's own research joins aging biology to mitochondrial disease, the inherited disorders in which the cell's power plants fail. One line of work asks what mTOR inhibition does in mitochondrial disease, including how the dose of an mTOR inhibitor shapes its effects on body weight and on the disease itself. Johnson studied biochemistry and biophysics at Oregon State University, earned the PhD in Molecular Basis of Disease at the University of Washington and was a postdoctoral fellow in genetics at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York.

Johnson then led a laboratory as Assistant Professor of Neurology at the University of Washington and Principal Investigator in the Center for Integrative Brain Research at Seattle Children's Research Institute, studying the molecular and developmental mechanisms of pediatric genetic disease, mainly mitochondrial disease. Johnson is now a professor in the School of Geography and Natural Sciences at Northumbria University in Newcastle, where the research interests listed are mitochondrial disease and biology, the basic biology of anaesthesia, biogerontology and the cell and molecular basis of human genetic disease. Oregon State University gave Johnson its Young Alumni Award in 2023.

highlights.JOH2013: First author: wrote the Nature review that set out the case for mTOR as a key modulator of aging and age-related disease across species.
